title: The Right Tool for the Right Hands
author: Andrew Cantarutti
summary: Andrew Cantarutti argues that schools systematically misapply EdTech evaluation frameworks by using the same efficiency standard for teacher-facing and student-facing tools -- a standard that makes sense for the former but fires badly when applied to the latter. His core distinction: teacher-facing tools should be evaluated for professional utility (do they free the teacher to do more of the work that requires human judgment?), while student-facing tools must be evaluated for developmental cost (what cognitive capacity does this tool displace that the student is still building?). Unlike teachers, who are formed professionals, students are in the middle of building the cognitive architecture that underpins everything else. The essay's key insight is that some tools -- particularly Learning Management Systems like Google Classroom -- are sold to teachers on efficiency grounds but function by routing student behavior through the platform, offloading executive function that students need to develop. The article provides a two-tier framework and practical talking points for making the case to administrators.
points: Teacher-facing tools should be evaluated for professional utility; student-facing tools must be evaluated for developmental cost -- these are categorically different standards, and conflating them produces decisions that help teachers while quietly harming students.

The clarifying question for any EdTech tool is whether its function depends on shaping or replacing student behavior -- if a tool is sold to teachers but only works by routing student cognitive processes through the platform, it must be evaluated as a student-facing tool.

LMSs like Google Classroom simultaneously save teachers time and outsource students' executive function (tracking deadlines, managing attention, organizing work) -- the teacher's convenience and the student's developmental cost are not separable; they are produced by the same features.

Routinely posting slides and notes for all students is not access support but a structural signal that being present and taking notes is optional -- and when schools remove this requirement, attendance itself begins to feel negotiable.

The argument that teacher convenience and student development are in competition is false -- they are only in conflict when we conflate the tools that serve each; separating them allows schools to protect both.
quotes: When a teacher posts a new assignment to Google Classroom, they know that their students have been notified. They know they're reaching students who happen to be absent that day. Students who receive notifications for new assignments learn that paying attention to in-class instructions is optional.
The convenience these tools afford is real, but so are the costs, and they don't fall on the same person.

Unlike the children we work with, teachers are formed professionals. Their administrative efficiency isn't a developmental capacity in formation. Time saved on grading logistics can be time returned to the work that requires astute human judgement.

Students are in the middle of building the cognitive architecture that underpins everything else. When a tool robs a student of the opportunity to sustain their attention, to exercise their working memory, or to organize their own work, it forecloses the repetition needed to build those key capacities.
Digital prostheses don't just complete tasks, they pilfer our students' chances to exercise the capacities they need to develop.

Having to be present, attentive, and responsible for capturing information is, in and of itself, a desirable difficulty, not an inconvenience. When schools remove this requirement in the name of access, they often fail to notice what they've traded away.
The tools that genuinely help teachers are almost never sold on that basis alone. They're almost always marketed as catalysts of student learning, but that claim rarely survives scrutiny.
